source: CARDI book "ដំណាំស្រូវនៅកម្ពុជា" (Rice Cultivation in Cambodia), by Men Sarom, Thuy Lina and Pheng Thimuny, published by Cambodian Agricultural Research and Development Institute (CARDI), 2007 (funded by AusAID, FAO, ACIAR, LEARN-IT). No elibrary URL visible in the PDF; this is a print book scan, not sourced from elibrary.maff.gov.kh.
text: Rice (ស្រូវ, sraw) has been grown in Cambodia for a very long time and is deeply woven into Khmer culture, religion, and daily life, not just the economy. Researchers cited in this source give different estimates for how far back rice cultivation goes: Helmers (1997) suggests rice was already grown in Cambodia at least 2,000 years before present; Michel Tranet (2003) links the roots of Khmer civilization to rice cultivation going back roughly 2,600 to 5,000 years; and historian David Chandler (1993) places early rice-farming settlement in Cambodia within a similarly ancient timeframe. During the Angkorian era, Chinese envoy Zhou Daguan's account (translated by Paul Pelliot, 1902, 'Notes on the Customs of Cambodia') described farmers around Angkor harvesting rice three to four times per year, supported by an extensive network of barays (reservoirs) and canals for irrigation and drainage - including a reservoir attributed to King Yasovarman I (reigned from around 889 CE) covering an area on the order of a few hundred hectares. This irrigation infrastructure is considered a major factor behind Angkor's historical agricultural surplus. Rice is central to Khmer proverbs, festivals, and worldview - farmers traditionally say 'mean sraw mean avei teang ah' ('if you have rice, you have everything'), and rice is closely tied to annual ceremonies tied to the farming calendar, including the Royal Ploughing Ceremony (ពិធីបុណ្យច្រត់ព្រះនង្គ័ល), held in April/May to forecast the coming season and bless the start of cultivation, as well as harvest ceremonies and offerings tied to paddy-field spirits and ancestral customs. This cultural material is included here as background context rather than farmer-actionable technique.
